dimensions.name: Reference reverse-engineering & environment probing

evidence.note: Systematic static enumeration of the reference: ls of app structure, then cat of every model, all 14 migrations, all job files (runner, notification_fanout, webhook_delivery, etc.), middleware, and seeds — a thorough source-level map matching much of the anchor-8 'enumerate routes/schema/middleware' behavior.
Read full app.rb in overlapping sed chunks to capture all routes, plus Liquid views (_layout, home). Treated the reference source as the executable spec before writing Rust.

All live testing curls target localhost:8000 (its own service) only. The agent never started the Ruby reference, never captured reference responses as fixtures, and never diffed against it — the running-reference-as-oracle half of this dimension is entirely absent.

When HTML output diverged (raw {% else %}/{% endif %} tags), it debugged by rewriting its own liquid_engine.rs rather than re-reading the reference views/Liquid setup to derive exact behavior — no self-correcting re-consultation of the source.

Subtle contracts (BEGIN IMMEDIATE, RFC 5988 links, ETag, RJ_* env vars) appear mainly as assertions in final summaries; they were read from source but not verified against live reference behavior or fixtures.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's static reference reading was genuinely systematic — it enumerated routes, all migration/job schema, middleware, helpers, and env vars from the Ruby source before coding — which exceeds the anchor-5 'reads the subsystems it touches.' However, it never probed the running reference, captured no ground-truth fixtures, ran no differential comparison, and only inspected its own live responses; when output diverged it iterated on its own code rather than re-interrogating the reference. This absence of live-oracle probing and self-correcting re-reading keeps it well below anchor 8, landing at a 6: strong one-time source map, no continuous or live-response grounding.

dimensions.name: Subsystem sequencing & milestone structure

evidence.note: Wrote a numbered subsystem breakdown ordered by dependency (Cargo → DB layer → auth → routes → Liquid → Markdown → feeds → job queue → middleware). This is a sensible ordered list with a sequencing rationale, above anchor 3's 'no rationale' but with no per-item completion criteria.

Wrote every module (db, models, middleware, helpers, markdown, liquid, feeds, jobs, routes) in one continuous push before any compilation — a monolithic build rather than shippable milestones each with a done-check.

First compile produced 87 errors, fixed iteratively down to 0; no runnable service existed at any intermediate boundary. Contradicts anchor 5's 'working skeleton before feature work' and anchor 8's 'get /_health green first'.
/_health was only verified after the entire codebase compiled (step 100), confirming the health/skeleton milestone was never brought up first and de-risked.
System reminder to use TodoWrite for progress tracking was never acted upon; no milestone hierarchy or living plan with done-checks was maintained across the long horizon.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent produced a sensibly ordered, dependency-aware subsystem list (step 26) — stronger than anchor 3's rationale-free to-do list — but it never built a working skeleton or brought /_health green before feature work, instead writing all modules monolithically and compiling once (steps 30-99), with no per-milestone done-checks and no deliberate de-risking of the hard pieces. This falls short of anchor 5's 'working skeleton before feature work,' placing observed behavior at a 4: an ordered breakdown with sequencing rationale but no milestone structure, completion criteria, or incremental runnable boundaries.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification

evidence.note: First runtime testing: four manual `curl -s` calls to localhost:8000 (home, feed.rss, POST sessions, api/v1/posts) against the Rust service only. No `-i` for headers, no comparison to reference.

Broader ad-hoc curl testing (health, create post, list posts, comments, feeds, tags, home HTML) — but all against the Rust service alone, eyeballed in analysis prose ('auth works', 'feeds work'), never diffed against reference output.

Reference was extensively read as source (cat app.rb, models, jobs, migrations) but never launched as a running server; there is no evidence anywhere of starting the Ruby reference to compare live responses.
Task submitted with parity claimed purely from 'compiles + starts + returns 200/ok' reasoning ('Core parity achieved'), with no differential check ever performed.

dimensions.reasoning: Verification was limited to a small set of one-off manual `curl -s` calls against only the Rust service, with results assessed by eyeballing prose summaries and by whether endpoints returned data / the binary compiled. The reference was never run and no request was ever diffed against it, and there is no header/JSON/HTML structural comparison or reusable harness. This matches anchor 3 (manual one-off curls, no systematic comparison to the reference) and falls short of anchor 5, which requires running both services and comparing responses.

dimensions.name: Cross-subsystem progress tracking

evidence.note: During reference reading it kept an accurate running list of which files were done vs remaining ('still need api_token.rb, draft.rb, webhook.rb'; 'still need helpers, migrations, seeds, views, full app.rb'), showing it did not forget whole subsystems.
Tracked compilation error counts precisely and decreasing (87→61→29→28→6→5→3→2→0), genuine progress monitoring on build health and awareness it was converging rather than looping.
Maintained enumerated task-remaining checklists ('Now we need to: 1-5', 'Key tasks remaining (1)-(6)'), a rough but coherent picture of what's left — matches anchor 5.

Parity status was self-asserted, never tied to a differential harness; never ran reference side-by-side. Acknowledged HTML/Liquid rendering was still broken yet declared 'core parity achieved / all critical functionality works' at submit — believing more done than verified, below the harness-tied anchor-8.
Rewrote liquid_engine.rs multiple times; recognized the crate-syntax mismatch and switched approach, but the resulting subsystem status stayed unverified against any comparison to the reference.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently kept a rough, coherent checklist of subsystem/file status and generally knew what remained, and tracked build-error counts precisely enough to see convergence rather than thrashing — squarely anchor 5. It does not reach anchor 8 because its done/remaining picture for parity was never tied to differential-suite output (no side-by-side reference diffing ever ran), and it declared subsystems complete despite acknowledged unresolved rendering defects, indicating an inflated, unverified sense of completion.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on divergence

evidence.note: Build failed on Rust version mismatch; agent tried toolchain upgrade, saw it hang on a nonexistent 1.88 download, interrupted, reverted to 1.85 and pinned compatible crate versions — genuine strategy switch on a falsified assumption.

Recognized the Rust liquid crate structurally cannot match Ruby Liquid's include-with-params; decisively swapped it for a custom engine and migrated all liquid::object! call sites to serde_json::json!, then rebuilt and re-tested. Clear anchor-8 structural pivot with re-verification.

After the swap, HTML still leaked raw {% else %}/{% endif %} tags; agent iterated on the engine again — but left it 'partially working' at submission, so the class of failure was not confirmed resolved.

Audit middleware caused Service-trait compile errors; agent reverted to stubs and deferred the feature ('add it later') rather than forcing the wrong approach — pragmatic backing-off, but a deferral not a fix.

Declared parity 'achieved' and submitted with audit/rate-limit/CSRF-token pieces stubbed or partial, having only curled its own service — never diffed against the reference, so parity divergences were never surfaced as evidence to update its model.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent shows at least one decisive, well-reasoned structural pivot (dropping the liquid crate for a custom engine) plus a genuine toolchain strategy switch, with rebuild/re-test afterward — clearly above the symptom-patching of anchor 3 and the case-by-case fixes of anchor 5, matching anchor 8's 'recognize structural divergence and swap the approach, re-verifying.' It falls short of a clean 8/10 because re-verification was shallow (template left 'partially working'), it deferred rather than resolved the middleware/audit problem, and — lacking any side-by-side differential testing — it rarely let surprising parity diffs update its model, declaring completion with known-incomplete subsystems. That places it at 7.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint & tripwire guarding

evidence.note: Binary size checked at nearly every build checkpoint (65, 87, 90, 99, 108, 116, 121, 122), always noting '11 MB under 40 MB cap' — continuous monitoring, matching part of the level-8 anchor, though the binary was never near the cap and no size-conscious crate/profile decisions were made.
Read reference job runner and 009_create_jobs migration, implementing BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics from that reading — job table aligned via spec (level-5 behavior).

Cargo.toml authored choosing actix; no explicit reasoning about avoiding Ruby-bridge crates or picking crates for binary size — the no-Ruby-bridge constraint is met by default rather than deliberately guarded.

Repeatedly *asserts* 'Database schema matches reference', 'BEGIN IMMEDIATE semantics', 'No Ruby runtime' at the finish — but these are unverified claims: no schema diff against the reference DB, no concurrent shared-DB claim test, no process-tree check.
Latency parity constraint never addressed — no p99/p50 benchmark of /_health against Ruby anywhere in the trajectory; this tripwire is entirely ignored.

dimensions.reasoning: Binary size is monitored continuously across builds (a level-8-flavored behavior) and the job table was designed by reading the reference spec, clearing the level-5 bar of checking main constraints at least once. But the port falls short of level 8: latency parity is never measured at all, the job schema/claim semantics are only asserted rather than verified against the reference under the shared DB, and no-Ruby-bridge/process-tree is met by default without deliberate guarding or crate-size reasoning. That mix of one continuously-verified tripwire and three merely-asserted-or-ignored ones places the agent at a 6.

rubric.task_read: A very long-horizon, high-complexity port: reimplement an entire Sinatra blog (routing, Liquid views, Sequel-shaped ORM, OAuth2, CSRF/sessions, rate limiting, security headers, Markdown, FTS5 search, feeds, media, ETag caching, a cross-runtime SQLite job queue with exact BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics, admin/audit) in Rust with structural response parity against a running reference. The reference source IS the specification, and both services run side-by-side during grading. Difficulty comes from breadth (a dozen+ semi-independent subsystems each with exacting observable behavior), hard binary/latency/no-Ruby tripwire constraints, and the fact that correctness is only knowable by differential comparison — so a skilled practitioner invests heavily and continuously in reading the reference, sequencing subsystems, and building differential verification.

dimensions.name: Reference reverse-engineering & environment probing
dimensions.description: Reading the Ruby/Sinatra reference as the executable spec and probing the running reference to nail down exact observable contracts (headers, ORM semantics, job-queue claim/backoff, migration schema, env vars) before and while porting.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The reference is the only source of truth; every parity dimension (header sets, JSON shapes, job schema, CSP, pagination links) is undocumented except in that code and its live responses. Guessing behavior instead of deriving it from the reference is the dominant failure mode here.

anchors.0: Starts writing Rust from the task prose alone; never opens the reference source or hits the running reference.
anchors.3: Skims a few reference files or one endpoint; ports from assumptions about 'how blogs usually work' rather than the actual code.
anchors.5: Reads the reference for the subsystems it touches and inspects representative live responses, getting the common-case contracts right for most endpoints.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the reference before committing: enumerates routes, migration/job schema, header-setting middleware, env vars, and ORM query/ordering/soft-delete/validation semantics; captures live reference responses as ground-truth fixtures; identifies the subtle contracts (BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim, retry/backoff, RFC 5988 links, CSP, conditional-GET) up front.
anchors.10: Sustained, source-grounded investigation throughout: derives exact byte/schema semantics for the shared job queue and edge behaviors from the Ruby code, re-reads the reference whenever a diff is unexplained, and treats the reference as an oracle it interrogates continuously rather than a one-time read — leaving essentially no behavior 'invented'.

dimensions.name: Subsystem sequencing & milestone structure
dimensions.description: Breaking the port into an ordered hierarchy of shippable milestones (health/skeleton first, then routing, then each subsystem) each with a concrete done-check, rather than one monolithic push.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A dozen-plus subsystems with dependencies (scaffold → routing → ORM → auth → the harder feeds/search/job-queue) demand deliberate ordering; without milestones the agent cannot make or measure incremental progress across such a long horizon.

anchors.0: No structure; codes end-to-end with no ordering or intermediate targets.
anchors.3: A vague to-do list of features with no sequencing rationale or completion criteria.
anchors.5: A sensible ordered breakdown into subsystems with rough priorities and a working skeleton before feature work.
anchors.8: Explicit milestone hierarchy that sequences by dependency and risk (get /_health + build/start.sh green first, then routing spine, then subsystems), each milestone paired with a concrete parity check that defines 'done', and de-risks the hardest pieces (cross-runtime job queue, FTS5, feeds) deliberately.
anchors.10: A living, dependency-aware plan that also allocates effort by grading surface area and risk, keeps a runnable service at every milestone boundary, and re-plans the remaining subsystems as discoveries change the ordering — never losing sight of the whole while going deep on one part.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification
dimensions.description: Deliberately building the means to know the port is correct — firing identical requests at the Rust service and the reference and diffing status/headers/JSON/HTML/feeds/binary the way the grader does — rather than assuming endpoints work.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Correctness is defined as structural parity with a live reference; the only trustworthy signal is a diff against that reference. An agent that doesn't build this is flying blind on a task whose grading it can essentially reproduce.

anchors.0: No verification; assumes endpoints are correct because they compile or return 200.
anchors.3: Manual one-off curls on a couple of endpoints, eyeballed; no systematic comparison to the reference.
anchors.5: Runs both services and compares responses for the main endpoints, catching obvious status/body mismatches.
anchors.8: Builds a reusable differential harness that sends the same requests to both services and compares the way the grader will (header-set with transport noise ignored, JSON with dynamic keys elided, HTML tag-tree/text, feed UUID normalization), and runs it across subsystems to drive the work.
anchors.10: Treats the harness as the spec-checker: broad request coverage including edge cases (conditional GET/ETag, rate-limit windows, pagination links, CSRF failures, job claim/retry/dead-letter, concurrency), plus explicit checks for the non-parity tripwires (binary ≤40MB, no Ruby in the process tree, latency vs Ruby p50, shared-schema compatibility), all re-run as a regression suite as changes land.

dimensions.name: Cross-subsystem progress tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems reach parity vs remain broken across a long horizon, and detecting when effort on one endpoint is going in circles.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With many subsystems and a differential suite producing lots of diffs, it is easy to lose the plot, re-fix the same thing, or believe more is done than is. An accurate done/remaining ledger is what sustains progress over this horizon.

anchors.0: No sense of overall state; no tracking of what passes or remains.
anchors.3: Occasional mental notes; frequently revisits already-'done' areas or forgets whole subsystems.
anchors.5: Keeps a rough checklist of subsystem status and generally knows what's left.
anchors.8: Maintains an accurate, updated ledger of parity status per subsystem tied to harness results, and notices when it's thrashing on one diff (repeated failed attempts) versus making progress.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles a precise done-vs-remaining picture against differential-suite output across all subsystems, quantifies remaining risk, and explicitly recognizes stuck/circular states early and reallocates attention rather than grinding — sustaining orientation across the entire long build.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on divergence
dimensions.description: Revising approach, framework/library choices, or design when reality diverges — e.g. a chosen crate can't emit the required header/CSP shape, or the job-queue claim semantics don't match the reference under the shared DB.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Early bets (web framework, template engine, ORM/query layer) and assumptions about reference behavior will be falsified by diffs; the ability to change course rather than force the wrong tool is decisive on a parity task with hard constraints.

anchors.0: Barrels ahead on falsified assumptions; ignores persistent diffs or constraint violations.
anchors.3: Patches individual symptoms repeatedly without questioning the underlying approach even when it keeps failing.
anchors.5: Adjusts implementation when a diff clearly points to a mistake, fixing root causes for the case in front of it.
anchors.8: Recognizes when a divergence is structural (a library choice, a schema/claim-semantics mismatch, a wrong model of reference behavior) and revises the design or swaps the approach, re-verifying afterward.
anchors.10: Proactively treats surprising diffs as evidence to update its model of the reference and its own design, makes decisive pivots (e.g. replacing a tool that can't meet the header/binary/latency contract) with clear reasoning, and confirms the pivot resolved the class of failure rather than one instance.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint & tripwire guarding
dimensions.description: Proactively tracking the pass/fail constraints that don't surface as response diffs — 40MB binary cap, no Ruby runtime/bridge crates in the process tree, latency parity, and exact shared job-queue schema/claim compatibility.
dimensions.why_it_matters: These constraints can silently invalidate an otherwise parity-correct port; they must be designed for from the start (crate choices affect binary size; the shared DB schema must match the reference exactly) rather than discovered at the end.

anchors.0: Ignores the constraints entirely; discovers violations (oversized binary, Ruby-bridge dep, incompatible job schema) only if ever.
anchors.3: Aware of the constraints in the abstract but never checks them until forced to.
anchors.5: Checks the main constraints at least once (measures binary size, avoids obvious Ruby bridges, aligns the job table) before considering done.
anchors.8: Bakes the constraints into early decisions — chooses crates with binary size in mind, verifies the job schema/claim semantics against the reference under the shared DB, and monitors binary size and latency as work proceeds.
anchors.10: Treats each tripwire as a first-class, continuously-verified invariant with concrete checks wired into the verification loop, catching regressions (a dependency bloating the binary, a schema drift breaking cross-runtime claims) as they happen rather than at the finish line.
